questions.stem: Washington's attack on Hessian troops at Trenton on 26 December 1776 was significant mainly because it:
options: persuaded France to sign an alliance with the United States that same week
ended the war in the northern states and shifted all fighting to the south
revived Patriot morale after a run of defeats in New York and New Jersey
forced the British to abandon New York City and withdraw to Canada
questions.explanation: After losing New York and retreating across New Jersey, the Continental Army was close to collapse; Trenton, and Princeton soon after, restored confidence and encouraged enlistment. The British held New York until 1783, and the French alliance came in 1778.

questions.stem: Which battle of October 1777 is usually seen as the turning point of the war because it helped bring France into an alliance with the United States?
options: Yorktown
Bunker Hill
Long Island
Saratoga
questions.explanation: Burgoyne's surrender at Saratoga convinced France that the Americans could win, and the Franco-American alliance was signed in February 1778. Yorktown, in 1781, was the last major battle rather than the turning point.

questions.stem: The winter at Valley Forge (1777–78) is significant in the history of the Continental Army because:
options: despite shortages, the army emerged better trained under Baron von Steuben
the army won its first victory there over British regulars under General Howe
the soldiers mutinied and forced Congress to pay them in gold and silver coin
Washington resigned his command there and was replaced by Horatio Gates
questions.explanation: Hunger, cold and disease killed many men at Valley Forge, yet Steuben's drilling made the army more effective. No battle was fought there, and Washington kept command throughout the war.

questions.stem: What was the role of France in the American victory at Yorktown in 1781?
options: France blockaded London and forced Parliament to end the war
French troops and a French fleet helped trap Cornwallis's army
France negotiated Cornwallis's surrender in return for Canada
France paid British troops to abandon their positions in Virginia
questions.explanation: Rochambeau's French army fought alongside Washington, and de Grasse's fleet stopped the Royal Navy from rescuing Cornwallis, who surrendered on 19 October 1781. French money and naval power were vital to American victory.

questions.stem: Under the Treaty of Paris of 1783, Britain:
options: kept control of all lands west of the Appalachians
agreed to pay compensation for wartime damage
kept the right to tax American trade with Europe
recognised the independence of the United States
questions.explanation: Britain recognised American independence, with a western boundary at the Mississippi River and fishing rights off Newfoundland. Britain paid no compensation, and Congress agreed only to recommend that states restore Loyalist property.

questions.stem: Which group gained least from the terms of the Treaty of Paris 1783?
options: Native American nations, whose lands were handed to the United States
American farmers, who gained access to land as far west as the Mississippi River
New England fishermen, who kept their rights to fish off Newfoundland
British merchants, whose pre-war debts were to be recognised by Americans
questions.explanation: The treaty made no provision for Britain's Native American allies; their lands between the Appalachians and the Mississippi were simply transferred to the United States. Farmers, fishermen and British creditors all had interests protected in the treaty.

questions.stem: Under the Articles of Confederation, which power did Congress lack?
options: the power to borrow money
the power to levy taxes
the power to declare war
the power to make treaties
questions.explanation: Congress could make war and treaties and borrow money, but it could not tax; it could only request money from the states, which often failed to pay. This weakness lay behind many of the Confederation's problems.

questions.stem: Under the Articles of Confederation, each state in Congress had:
options: votes in proportion to its tax payments
a veto over all decisions of Congress
one vote, whatever its population
votes in proportion to its population
questions.explanation: Each state had a single vote, so small states counted as much as large ones; major measures needed nine of the thirteen states. This equal voting became a central dispute at the Philadelphia Convention.

questions.stem: In 1781 Congress proposed an amendment to the Articles allowing a 5 per cent duty on imports. Rhode Island alone rejected it, and it failed. This shows that:
options: amending the Articles required unanimity, so one state could block reform
the Articles let Congress tax imports but only with the consent of Rhode Island
Rhode Island held a veto over all laws because it was the smallest state
the states had agreed to abolish duties on imports and exports entirely
questions.explanation: Any amendment to the Articles needed the consent of all thirteen states, so a single state's refusal defeated the impost. The episode showed reformers that the Articles could hardly be fixed from within.

questions.stem: Which was an achievement of the Confederation Congress?
options: The creation of a national army that crushed Shays' Rebellion
The creation of a single national currency that ended inflation
The ratification of the Bill of Rights by three-quarters of the states
The Northwest Ordinance of 1787, which set a path to statehood for western territories
questions.explanation: The Northwest Ordinance organised territory north of the Ohio River, provided for new states equal to the original ones and banned slavery there. Shays' Rebellion was put down by a privately funded Massachusetts militia, which itself showed Congress's weakness.

questions.stem: Which was a feature of the post-war recession of the 1780s?
options: The value of the Continental dollar rose sharply after the peace
British goods flooded in while Britain closed its West Indies trade
British loans to the states created a boom in American manufacturing
Congress set a high tariff that protected American industries
questions.explanation: After 1783 cheap British imports drained coin from the country while Britain shut American ships out of the British West Indies. Congress had no power to impose a tariff in retaliation, and Continental paper money had already collapsed in value.

questions.stem: In the 1780s some states, such as Rhode Island, passed laws issuing paper money and delaying debt collection. Who was most likely to oppose these laws?
options: Creditors such as merchants, who would be repaid in money worth less
Indebted farmers, who would be able to pay their debts more easily
State legislators who had been elected by indebted farmers
Former Continental soldiers who owed money on their farms
questions.explanation: Paper money and stay laws helped debtors at the expense of creditors, who were repaid in depreciated currency. Such laws alarmed men of property and persuaded many that a stronger national government was needed.

questions.stem: Shays' Rebellion (1786–87) was a revolt by farmers in western Massachusetts against:
options: the British troops who remained in western forts
the ratification of the federal Constitution
the Northwest Ordinance's ban on slavery
heavy state taxes and the seizure of property for debt
questions.explanation: Farmers, many of them veterans, closed courts to stop foreclosures for debt and taxes that had to be paid in coin. The rebellion came before the Constitution existed, and it was suppressed early in 1787.

questions.stem: Why did Shays' Rebellion strengthen the case for a new constitution?
options: It showed that Congress could not raise forces or money to keep order
It showed that the states had too little power over their own militias
It showed that the British still controlled the western frontier
It showed that the Articles gave Congress too much power over taxes
questions.explanation: Congress could not fund troops, so Massachusetts relied on a militia paid for by Boston merchants. Leaders such as Washington and Madison saw the revolt as proof that the Confederation was too weak to protect property and order.

questions.stem: Writing to James Madison in January 1787, Thomas Jefferson said that 'a little rebellion now and then is a good thing'. This view of Shays' Rebellion differs from Washington's because Jefferson:
options: supported the rebels' demand that Massachusetts abolish its state legislature
believed the revolt proved the need for a king, where Washington disagreed
wanted Congress to raise a national army to crush the rebels at once
saw such unrest as a healthy check on rulers, where Washington saw danger
questions.explanation: Jefferson, then in Paris, thought occasional resistance kept rulers alert to the people. Washington was alarmed and saw the rebellion as evidence of anarchy that a stronger government must prevent. Neither supported a monarchy.

questions.stem: The Virginia Plan, drafted largely by James Madison, proposed a national legislature in which:
options: each state would have one vote, as under the Articles
each state would have two senators and no lower house
members would be appointed for life by the president
representation in both houses would be based on population
questions.explanation: The Virginia Plan favoured the large states by basing representation on population. The New Jersey Plan, by contrast, kept equal votes for each state.

questions.stem: The Connecticut (Great) Compromise at the Philadelphia Convention settled the dispute over representation by providing that:
options: both houses would reflect population, but small states could veto laws
both houses would give each state one vote, as under the Articles
the House would reflect population and each state would have two senators
the House would have equal state votes and the Senate would reflect population
questions.explanation: The compromise combined the two plans: representation by population in the House of Representatives and equal representation, two senators per state, in the Senate. The second option reverses the arrangement.

questions.stem: The Three-fifths Compromise at the Philadelphia Convention provided that:
options: enslaved people would be freed after three-fifths of their term of service
three-fifths of Congress would be needed to override a presidential veto
three-fifths of enslaved people counted for seats and direct taxes
three-fifths of the states would be needed to ratify the new Constitution
questions.explanation: Southern states wanted enslaved people counted to increase their representation; the compromise counted three-fifths of them. Ratification needed nine of thirteen states, and a veto override needs two-thirds of both houses.

questions.stem: Which statement about slavery in the Constitution of 1787 is accurate?
options: The slave trade was protected until 1808, and escapees had to be returned
The Constitution abolished slavery in the northern states but kept it in the south
The Constitution banned the importation of slaves from the date it was ratified
The word 'slavery' appears in the Constitution's description of citizenship
questions.explanation: The Constitution protected the slave trade until 1808 and required the return of people 'held to Service or Labour' who escaped to another state. It avoids the words 'slave' and 'slavery'. Northern abolition came through state action, not the Constitution.

questions.stem: Which feature of the Constitution is an example of checks and balances?
options: Each state has two senators chosen by its state legislature
The House of Representatives is elected every two years
Ratification required the approval of nine state conventions
The president may veto bills, but Congress can override by a two-thirds vote
questions.explanation: The veto and the override let each branch limit the other, the essence of checks and balances. The other features concern how Congress is composed and how the Constitution was ratified, not one branch checking another.

questions.stem: Which change from the Articles of Confederation most directly answered the weaknesses exposed in the 1780s?
options: The states gained a veto over any law passed by the new Congress
Each state kept one equal vote in a single-chamber Congress
Amendments to the Constitution now required the agreement of every state
Congress gained power to levy taxes and regulate interstate and foreign commerce
questions.explanation: The Constitution gave Congress the powers it had lacked, to tax and to regulate commerce, and created an executive and federal courts. The other options describe the old system or make amendment harder; Article V needs three-quarters of the states, not all of them.

questions.stem: Who presided over the Philadelphia Convention of 1787?
options: George Washington
James Madison
Alexander Hamilton
Patrick Henry
questions.explanation: Washington's presence as president of the Convention lent it prestige. Madison was its leading thinker and kept the fullest notes, and Patrick Henry refused to attend.

questions.stem: Which argument was made by Anti-Federalists against the proposed Constitution?
options: It failed to create a president strong enough to act in a crisis
It made the Senate too small to represent the interests of the large states
It lacked a bill of rights and made the central government too powerful
It gave the states too much power and left the national government weak
questions.explanation: Anti-Federalists feared that a strong, distant government would swallow the states and threaten liberty, especially without a bill of rights. Federalists, not their opponents, complained about weak central government under the Articles.

questions.stem: 'The Federalist' essays (1787–88), written under the name 'Publius', were the work of:
options: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay
Patrick Henry, George Mason and Richard Henry Lee
Thomas Jefferson, John Adams and Benjamin Franklin
George Washington, John Hancock and Samuel Adams
questions.explanation: Hamilton, Madison and Jay wrote the essays to win support for ratification in New York. Henry and Mason were leading Anti-Federalists, and Jefferson was in France at the time.

questions.stem: In Federalist No. 10, James Madison argued that a large republic would protect liberty better than a small one because:
options: its size would let it raise a standing army against rebellions like Shays'
so many competing interests would stop any one faction forming a majority
it would be ruled by one strong president able to suppress dangerous factions
its states would each be small enough for citizens to govern directly
questions.explanation: Madison argued that factions cannot be removed without destroying liberty, but in an extended republic so many interests compete that no single faction can easily dominate. This turned the Anti-Federalist claim, that republics must be small, on its head.

questions.stem: In Federalist No. 51, Madison wrote that 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition'. He was defending:
options: the election of senators directly by the people
the power of Congress to override decisions of the courts
the separation of powers, with checks between the branches
the right of states to leave the Union if they chose
questions.explanation: Madison argued that each branch should have the means and motive to resist encroachment by the others, so that power checks power. The same essay observes that 'if men were angels, no government would be necessary'.

questions.stem: How many of the thirteen states had to ratify the Constitution for it to take effect among them?
options: thirteen
nine
seven
ten
questions.explanation: Article VII required ratification by conventions in nine states. Requiring all thirteen, as the Articles did for amendments, would have let one state block it; New Hampshire became the ninth in June 1788.

questions.stem: Several states, including Massachusetts, ratified the Constitution while recommending amendments. The main long-term result was that:
options: Federalists agreed to support a bill of rights once the government began
the Constitution was rewritten by a second convention before it took effect
the new Congress abolished the Senate in response to the states' objections
ratification was cancelled until all thirteen states had approved it
questions.explanation: To win close votes, Federalists promised to consider amendments after ratification, and Madison then guided the Bill of Rights through the First Congress. No second convention was held.

questions.stem: In 1789 the First Congress approved amendments that became the Bill of Rights. Who introduced them in the House of Representatives?
options: James Madison
Alexander Hamilton
Patrick Henry
John Jay
questions.explanation: Madison had once thought a bill of rights unnecessary but introduced amendments in June 1789 to answer Anti-Federalist fears; Congress approved them in September 1789, and ten were ratified by 1791. Henry, an Anti-Federalist, was not in Congress.

questions.stem: Which right is protected by the First Amendment?
options: Freedom of speech and of the press
The right to keep and bear arms
The right to a speedy public trial
Protection from unreasonable searches
questions.explanation: The First Amendment protects freedom of religion, speech, the press, assembly and petition. Bearing arms is the Second Amendment, unreasonable searches the Fourth and a speedy trial the Sixth.

questions.stem: The Tenth Amendment states that powers not given to the federal government, nor prohibited to the states, are reserved to the states or the people. It was intended to:
options: give the federal government power over any matter the states neglected
allow the states to cancel federal laws they considered unconstitutional
abolish the powers of the states over their own militias and courts
reassure those who feared the federal government would absorb the states
questions.explanation: The Tenth Amendment answered Anti-Federalist fears of consolidation by confirming that the federal government held only the powers it was given. It does not let states cancel federal laws; the Constitution makes federal law supreme.

questions.stem: At Newburgh in March 1783, some army officers threatened action against Congress over unpaid wages. How did Washington respond?
options: He led the officers to Philadelphia to force Congress to pay
He resigned his command in protest at Congress's failure
He had the leading officers arrested and shot for mutiny
He persuaded the officers to stay loyal to civilian authority
questions.explanation: Washington addressed the officers, famously putting on his spectacles and remarking that he had grown grey in their service, and they backed down. His insistence on civilian control, confirmed when he resigned his commission in December 1783, shaped the new republic.

questions.stem: Alexander Hamilton contributed to the creation of the new political system by:
options: refusing to attend the Philadelphia Convention in protest at its aims
pressing for a stronger national government and writing many Federalist essays
leading the Anti-Federalists in the New York ratifying convention
drafting the Articles of Confederation in 1777 to protect the powers of the states
questions.explanation: Hamilton helped call the Philadelphia Convention, wrote most of 'The Federalist' and led the fight for ratification in New York, becoming the first Secretary of the Treasury in 1789. He was a leading Federalist, not an opponent of the Constitution.

questions.stem: At the Virginia ratifying convention of 1788, Patrick Henry objected to the Constitution's opening words, asking what right its framers had to say 'We, the people'. His objection was that:
options: the Constitution's preamble should have named George Washington as the first president
the Constitution's framers had been elected by the people rather than by the states
the Constitution made a consolidated national government, not a union of states
the Constitution gave the vote to every adult, including women and enslaved people
questions.explanation: Henry argued that the framers, sent by the states, had no authority to speak for one American people, and that 'We, the people' signalled a consolidated government that would destroy the states' sovereignty. The framers were in fact chosen by state legislatures.

questions.stem: James Madison is often called the 'Father of the Constitution' because he:
options: shaped the Virginia Plan, kept the fullest notes and defended the result in print
wrote every article of the Constitution himself and signed it alone
presided over the Philadelphia Convention and cast the deciding votes
drafted the Articles of Confederation and later amended them himself
questions.explanation: Madison prepared the Virginia Plan that set the Convention's agenda, recorded its debates and co-wrote 'The Federalist'. Washington presided; the Constitution was the work of many delegates and compromises.

questions.stem: Which was a common experience of Loyalists during and after the War of Independence?
options: They were protected by the Treaty of Paris, which restored all their property
They were required to serve in the Continental Army to prove their loyalty
Many had property confiscated and left for British North America or Britain
Most were given seats in the new state legislatures as a reward for neutrality
questions.explanation: Loyalists faced harassment, confiscation and banishment, and tens of thousands left for places such as Nova Scotia, Quebec and Britain. The Treaty of Paris only had Congress recommend restitution, which most states ignored.

questions.stem: In March 1776 Abigail Adams wrote to her husband John asking Congress to 'remember the ladies'. What was the outcome for women's rights in the period to 1789?
options: Women were admitted as delegates to the state ratifying conventions
Their legal status changed little, though their role raising citizens was praised
Women gained the vote in federal elections under the Constitution of 1787
Congress gave married women full rights to own property and make contracts in their own names
questions.explanation: Married women remained under coverture, without separate legal identity, and could not vote, except briefly for some property-owning women in New Jersey. Historian Linda Kerber called the new ideal of women raising virtuous citizens 'Republican Motherhood'.

questions.stem: How did most Native American nations respond to the War of Independence?
options: Most joined the Continental Army in return for promises of land in the west
Most stayed united and neutral, so the war did not affect their homelands
Most moved west of the Mississippi before fighting reached their territory
Most sided with Britain, seeing the colonists as the greater threat
questions.explanation: Many nations allied with Britain, which had tried to limit settlement since 1763. The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy split, with the Oneida and Tuscarora aiding the Patriots, and American campaigns such as Sullivan's in 1779 destroyed many towns.

questions.stem: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 promised that the 'utmost good faith shall always be observed towards the Indians' and that their lands would not be taken without consent. A historian evaluating this source would most likely note that:
options: it was the first treaty ever signed between Congress and the Haudenosaunee
it gave Native Americans citizenship and representation in Congress
it reserved all land north of the Ohio River for Native Americans for ever
settlement and land cessions continued, so the promise was not kept in practice
questions.explanation: The Ordinance states an ideal, but it was written to organise the sale and settlement of Native lands, and dispossession continued through pressured treaties and war. Comparing stated intentions with outcomes is central to evaluating such a source.

questions.stem: Lord Dunmore's Proclamation of November 1775 offered freedom to enslaved people who:
options: left Patriot masters and fought for the British
fought for the Continental Army under Washington
bought their freedom from their Loyalist masters
moved north to states that had abolished slavery
questions.explanation: Dunmore, royal governor of Virginia, offered freedom to enslaved people of rebels who joined British forces, and thousands of African Americans fled to the British during the war. Many Black Loyalists later settled in Nova Scotia.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the extent of change for African Americans between 1776 and 1789?
options: Slavery was abolished across the United States by the Constitution and the Bill of Rights
Nothing changed, since no state took any step towards ending slavery before 1789
Slavery ended in the south during the war, but northern states kept it until 1789
Northern states began ending slavery, but the Constitution protected it in the south
questions.explanation: Vermont, Pennsylvania (gradually from 1780) and Massachusetts moved to end slavery, and some southern owners freed slaves, but slavery remained central to the southern economy and the Constitution protected it. This mix of change and continuity is the key judgement.

questions.stem: Which experience was common for Continental Army soldiers?
options: They received generous land grants and pensions immediately after enlisting
They served only within their own state and could not be sent elsewhere
They were drafted from the wealthiest families, who could afford equipment
Pay arrived late, often in paper money or certificates that lost value
questions.explanation: Soldiers endured shortages of food and clothing and were paid late in depreciating currency or certificates, which many sold cheaply to speculators. Grievances led to mutinies, such as the Pennsylvania Line's in 1781. Many recruits were poor men attracted by bounties.

questions.stem: Which development from 1776 to 1789 is the strongest evidence of change rather than continuity in American society?
options: Virginia's 1786 Statute for Religious Freedom, ending compulsory support for any church
The continued exclusion of women from voting in almost every state
The continued leadership of wealthy landowners and merchants in politics
The continued expansion of settlement onto Native American lands
questions.explanation: Virginia's statute, drafted by Jefferson and carried by Madison, ended compulsory support for any church and broke with the colonial established Church. The other options describe continuities: women's exclusion, elite leadership and the westward pressure on Native lands all persisted.

questions.stem: Historian Charles Beard, in 'An Economic Interpretation of the Constitution' (1913), argued that:
options: the framers acted largely from economic interests, such as holding public debt
the framers were moved mainly by republican ideas of virtue drawn from Rome
the Constitution was a radical democratic document favouring indebted farmers
the Constitution was forced on the states by the British as a condition of peace
questions.explanation: Beard, a Progressive historian, argued that the framers' property and securities shaped a Constitution protecting creditors and property. Later historians challenged his evidence, but his thesis set a lasting debate about interests and ideals.

questions.stem: Gordon Wood, in 'The Radicalism of the American Revolution', argued that the revolution:
options: was mainly a conservative defence of colonial rights within the British Empire
was a class war in which poor farmers overthrew the colonial merchant elite
turned a hierarchical, monarchical society into a more democratic one
changed little, because the same elites ruled before and after independence
questions.explanation: Wood argued that, although there was little bloodshed, the revolution was radical in breaking down ties of deference and hierarchy and releasing a more democratic and commercial society. The view that little changed is the position he argued against.
